title: It’s Always Lettuce
gist: A cyclosporiasis outbreak that has sickened more than 7,100 people in Michigan alone, likely traced to iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms, is the latest in a long chain of leafy-green foodborne illness events. The structural causes are consumption volume, bagged-salad lot aggregation across farms, overhead spray irrigation with untreated surface water, the absence of any cooking 'kill step,' and lettuce's crevice-heavy texture that shelters pathogens from washing.

insights.claim: An expanding US cyclosporiasis outbreak has sickened more than 7,100 people in Michigan alone, likely caused by iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A named supplier attached to a five-figure case count creates immediate recall, litigation and retail-delisting exposure for that producer.
insights.locator: Salad is usually synonymous with healthy eating

insights.claim: Leafy greens have driven a repeating series of US outbreaks: 2022 multistate E. coli from romaine on Wendy's sandwiches, 173 norovirus cases at Illinois eatery D.C. Cobb's, 31 salmonella cases from BrightFarms packaged greens in 2021, and 167 E. coli infections in 2019 from romaine grown in California's Salinas Valley.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: This is a recurring structural hazard, not a tail event — leafy-green suppliers carry a chronic, repriceable liability rather than a one-off shock.
insights.locator: In fact, leafy greens are frequently implicated

insights.claim: The current event is not the first cyclospora outbreak tied to lettuce — in 2020 Fresh Express salad kits were linked to more than 700 cases of the parasite.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Prior precedent means the industry knew the specific pathogen-product pairing and did not close the gap — relevant to negligence claims and regulatory pressure.
insights.locator: This isn't even the first cyclospora outbreak linked to lettuce

insights.claim: The CDC estimates produce is responsible for almost half of reported US foodborne illness cases, with leafy vegetables topping the list.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
entities: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
insights.so_what: Quantifies where food-safety regulatory attention and capital spending should concentrate — fresh produce, not meat processing.
insights.locator: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates

insights.claim: Lettuce is the second-most-consumed vegetable in the US behind potatoes, appearing in essentially every fast food sandwich, wrap, sub and taco, which mechanically maximizes exposure when contamination occurs.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Volume alone makes lettuce the highest-consequence produce category for any quick-service restaurant supply chain.
insights.locator: One big reason is simply because lots of people eat it

insights.claim: Ready-to-eat salads and spring-mix blends carry acute risk because they combine multiple leafy green types sourced from different farms and locations, so a single contaminated input contaminates the entire bag and then propagates across many packaged lots.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Lot aggregation is the amplifier — the more a processor blends sources for margin, the wider its recall radius when one farm fails.
insights.locator: Those ready-to-eat salads and blends of spring mix

insights.claim: A 2025 Cornell University study of E. coli outbreaks in romaine found that much of the contamination originates from irrigation with untreated surface water applied through overhead spray systems that wet the leaves directly.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, addressable capital-equipment failure point rather than a diffuse hygiene problem — the target for any regulation or ag-tech retrofit market.
insights.locator: A 2025 study by researchers at Cornell University

insights.claim: Switching to irrigation systems that do not touch the leaves would lower contamination risk, but requires equipment upgrades and downtime — the economic reason growers have not made the change.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: The fix is known and capex-gated, so outbreaks continue until liability or regulation makes the retrofit cheaper than the risk — a potential ag-equipment demand catalyst.
insights.locator: There are ways to lower that risk

themes.theme: No kill step, and washing doesn't work

insights.claim: Because lettuce is eaten raw it never passes through a 'kill step' — heating, pasteurization or freezing — the food-manufacturing stage designed to eliminate pathogens, leaving no downstream remediation after field contamination.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Absence of a kill step means safety must be achieved upstream in the field — process controls in the plant cannot compensate.
insights.locator: Lettuce’s satisfying crunch is also what makes it prone

insights.claim: Lettuce's physical texture — many crevices and folds — gives tiny pathogens shelter that washing does not reach, according to Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Product morphology, not process discipline, is a hard limit on how safe a raw leafy green can be made.
insights.quote: Many lettuce types have a lot of crevices and folds,
insights.locator: The texture of lettuce is an additional factor

insights.claim: Prewashing procedures at manufacturing facilities do not reliably remove microbes that cling tightly to leaves, and cyclospora specifically has thick outer walls making it highly resistant to most food sanitizers — vigorous scrubbing is the recommended countermeasure.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: The 'triple-washed' label on bagged salad is not a meaningful safety guarantee against this class of parasite — a consumer-trust vulnerability for packaged salad brands.
insights.locator: Even prewashing procedures at manufacturing facilities

insights.claim: Epidemiologist Amira Roess of George Mason University frames the residual risk as fully transferred to the consumer: whatever remains on the lettuce after inadequate washing is ingested.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Public-health guidance shifting the burden to household washing is an implicit admission that supply-chain controls are failing.
insights.quote: If you don't wash these products well, you're going to end up ingesting whatever is on the lettuce,
insights.locator: says Amira Roess, an epidemiologist at George Mason University

top_entities: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
